edges.description: Ingested bacteria face gastric acid and must buffer their periplasm to reach the mucosal niche.
Acid survival gives motile bacteria time to penetrate mucus and colonize epithelial-surface niches.
Persistent colonization of the mucosal surface induces chronic gastric inflammatory infiltration.
Colonizing cagA-positive strains deliver the CagA effector into the underlying gastric epithelial cells.

edges.description: Colonizing cagA-positive strains deliver the CagA effector into the underlying gastric epithelial cells, where it is tyrosine-phosphorylated.
The mucosal inflammatory infiltrate is the histologic lesion recognised clinically as chronic active gastritis.
Antral-predominant, body-sparing gastritis increases gastrin release and acid secretion.
Significant gastric body gastritis reduces acid secretion.
Long-standing inflammation leads to loss of gastric glands.
Chronic infection-driven gastric lymphoid infiltration is the setting in which gastric MALT lymphoma arises.
The increased duodenal acid load produces duodenal ulcer disease.
Duodenal ulceration is a form of peptic ulcer disease.
Abdominal pain in H. pylori infection is linked to the presence of ulcer disease rather than to gastritis alone.
Marked hypochlorhydria is associated with increased gastric-cancer risk.
Atrophic mucosa is replaced by intestinal-type epithelium.
Deregulated beta-catenin transactivates CDX1 and induces the intestinal goblet-cell mucin MUC2 in gastric epithelial cells.

edges.description: Intestinal metaplasia is a premalignant stage of the atrophy-metaplasia-dysplasia cascade to intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma.
Crowded or low-sanitation households increase oral, gastric, and fecal contact with infected family members.

nodes.description: H. pylori is eradicated with a proton pump inhibitor or the potassium-competitive acid blocker vonoprazan plus two or three antibiotics. An empiric clarithromycin-based regimen (with amoxicillin or metronidazole) is used where clarithromycin resistance is low; bismuth-containing quadruple therapy (bismuth, metronidazole, and tetracycline) is first choice where resistance is high or after prior clarithromycin exposure.
nodes.id: Acid suppression plus multidrug eradication therapy

evidence.reference_title: Pharmacological considerations and step-by-step proposal for the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection in the year 2018.
evidence.snippet: Over the past 30 years, multidrug regimens consisting of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) and two or three antibiotics have been used in treating Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection.

evidence.reference_title: Role of Bismuth in the Eradication of Helicobacter pylori.
evidence.snippet: Greater than 90% eradication success can be obtained by bismuth-containing quadruple therapy.

nodes.description: When gastritis is antral-predominant and spares the gastric body, increased gastrin release increases gastric acid secretion and the acid load delivered to the duodenum.

evidence.reference_title: Alterations in gastric physiology in Helicobacter pylori infection: causes of different diseases or all epiphenomena?
evidence.snippet: When there is antral predominant, body-sparing gastritis, there is increased gastrin release and this is accompanied by increased acid secretion.

nodes.description: Translocated CagA binds E-cadherin independently of its tyrosine phosphorylation, impairing the E-cadherin/beta-catenin complex so that beta-catenin accumulates in the cytoplasm and nucleus.
nodes.id: CagA E-cadherin Binding and Beta-Catenin Release

evidence.reference_title: Helicobacter pylori CagA interacts with E-cadherin and deregulates the beta-catenin signal that promotes intestinal transdifferentiation in gastric epithelial cells.
evidence.snippet: The CagA/E-cadherin interaction impairs the complex formation between E-cadherin and beta-catenin, causing cytoplasmic and nuclear accumulation of beta-catenin.

nodes.description: Oral, gastric, or fecal exposure introduces H. pylori into a susceptible child's stomach, where surviving bacteria can enter the gastric mucus layer.

evidence.reference_title: Helicobacter pylori infection: detection, investigation, and management.
evidence.snippet: If untreated, H pylori infection is lifelong.

nodes.description: Colonization produces chronic active inflammation in the gastric mucosa; the distribution of gastritis across antrum and body then determines whether acid output is increased, decreased, or unchanged.

evidence.reference_title: The physiology and metabolism of the human gastric pathogen Helicobacter pylori.
evidence.snippet: It is recognized as the major aetiological factor in chronic active type B gastritis, and gastric and duodenal ulceration and as a risk factor for gastric cancer.

nodes.description: Gastritis is the near-universal tissue response to persistent H. pylori colonization, even when infection is clinically silent.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori in Pediatrics.
evidence.snippet: Children infected with H. pylori develop histologic chronic active gastritis despite the fact that they are generally asymptomatic.

nodes.description: Body-predominant gastritis or pangastritis reduces acid secretion and raises intragastric pH, which raises intragastric nitrite, lowers gastric juice ascorbic acid, and allows colonization by nitrosating bacteria.

evidence.reference_title: Alterations in gastric physiology in Helicobacter pylori infection: causes of different diseases or all epiphenomena?
evidence.snippet: The hypochlorhydria probably plays an important role in the carcinogenic process as high intragastric pH markedly raises intragastric nitrite levels, profoundly lowers gastric juice ascorbic acid and allows colonization by nitrosating bacteria.

nodes.description: Acid-peptic injury of the duodenal mucosa produces duodenal ulcer, the acid-hypersecretory branch of H. pylori disease.

evidence.reference_title: Alterations in gastric physiology in Helicobacter pylori infection: causes of different diseases or all epiphenomena?
evidence.snippet: Subjects in whom the infection produces acid hypersecretion develop duodenal ulcer disease due to the increased duodenal acid load.

nodes.description: Symptomatic H. pylori infection can present with dyspeptic epigastric pain. In children, a link between H. pylori gastritis and abdominal pain has been established only when gastric or duodenal ulcer disease is present.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori in Pediatrics.
evidence.snippet: there is no evidence demonstrating a link between H. pylori-associated gastritis and abdominal pain, except in rare cases in which gastric or duodenal ulcer disease is present.

nodes.description: Gastric mucosa transdifferentiates to an intestinal phenotype, a precancerous lesion from which intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma arises.

evidence.reference_title: Helicobacter pylori CagA interacts with E-cadherin and deregulates the beta-catenin signal that promotes intestinal transdifferentiation in gastric epithelial cells.
evidence.snippet: Intestinal metaplasia is a precancerous lesion of the stomach characterized by transdifferentiation of the gastric mucosa to an intestinal phenotype.

evidence.reference_title: Helicobacter pylori infection: detection, investigation, and management.
evidence.snippet: rarely, gastric atrophy with/without intestinal metaplasia (ie, both precursor lesions for gastric cancer)

nodes.description: Extranodal marginal-zone (MALT) lymphoma of the stomach is a neoplastic outcome of chronic H. pylori infection and is detailed in the MALT lymphoma entry.

evidence.reference_title: Helicobacter pylori infection: detection, investigation, and management.
evidence.snippet: children infected with H pylori may have gastritis, ulcers, mucosal-associated lymphoid type lymphoma

nodes.description: Chronic H. pylori inflammation causes loss of gastric glands, the first premalignant rung of the atrophy-metaplasia-dysplasia cascade.

evidence.reference_title: A comparative systematic review and meta-analysis on the diagnostic accuracy of non-invasive tests for Helicobacter pylori detection in elderly patients.
evidence.snippet: This Gram-negative, type I carcinogen microorganism induces chronic gastric mucosal inflammation, resulting in atrophic and metaplastic alterations.

nodes.description: H. pylori establishes a chronic mucus-layer reservoir overlying gastric epithelial cells; motility, urease, and adhesins help the organism resist gastric acid, avoid mucus flow, and persist at the epithelial surface.

evidence.reference_title: Factors that mediate colonization of the human stomach by Helicobacter pylori.
evidence.snippet: Colonization of gastric mucus is likely to be key to the establishment of chronic infection.

nodes.description: Poor childhood sanitation, household crowding, and residence with infected family members predispose to H. pylori acquisition.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori in Pediatrics.
evidence.snippet: Risk factors such as minimal education and low socio-economic status during childhood affect the prevalence.

nodes.description: Gastric or duodenal ulceration is a minority outcome of the chronic gastric infection.

evidence.reference_title: Helicobacter pylori infection: detection, investigation, and management.
evidence.snippet: Helicobacter pylori infection causes gastritis and peptic ulcers and is associated with the development of gastric cancer.

nodes.description: Translocated CagA is tyrosine-phosphorylated by Src family kinases and then binds and activates the SHP-2 phosphatase, inducing morphological transformation of gastric epithelial cells. This is the phosphorylation-dependent arm of CagA signaling, distinct from the phosphorylation-independent E-cadherin arm.

evidence.reference_title: Helicobacter pylori CagA interacts with E-cadherin and deregulates the beta-catenin signal that promotes intestinal transdifferentiation in gastric epithelial cells.
evidence.snippet: Tyrosine-phosphorylated CagA specifically binds to and activates SHP-2 phosphatase, thereby inducing cell-morphological transformation.

nodes.description: Gastric adenocarcinoma is a long-term malignant outcome of chronic H. pylori infection and is detailed in the gastric-cancer-specific entries.

evidence.reference_title: Effect of Helicobacter pylori Eradication on Gastric Cancer Prevention: Updated Report From a Randomized Controlled Trial With 26.5 Years of Follow-up.
evidence.snippet: Participants receiving H pylori treatment had a lower incidence of gastric cancer compared with their placebo counterparts (hazard ratio [HR], 0.57; 95% CI, 0.33-0.98).

nodes.description: Persistent H. pylori after empiric therapy is treated with a regimen that avoids reused clarithromycin and can be tailored to antibiotic susceptibility or common 23S rRNA, rdxA, pbp1A, and gyrA/B resistance mutations.

evidence.reference_title: Pharmacological considerations and step-by-step proposal for the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection in the year 2018.
evidence.snippet: Options after initial eradication failure include tailored therapy (choosing antibiotic combinations based on antibiotic susceptibility testing), empiric bismuth-containing quadruple therapy or triple levofloxacin-based therapy.

evidence.reference_title: Mutation-driven mechanisms underlying antibiotic resistance of Helicobacter pylori in Asia: A systematic review and meta-analysis (2000-2024).
evidence.snippet: Clarithromycin resistance in H. pylori is mainly driven by A2142G/A2143G mutations (19-34%), while metronidazole resistance exceeds 84% in East Asia via rdxA mutations.

nodes.description: Acidic periplasmic pH opens the UreI urea channel, letting gastric urea reach nickel-dependent cytoplasmic urease; ammonia production then buffers the periplasm and permits survival at the acidic gastric surface.

evidence.reference_title: The gastric biology of Helicobacter pylori.
evidence.snippet: Gastric juice urea is able to rapidly access intrabacterial urease when the periplasmic pH falls below approximately 6.2 owing to pH-gating of a urea channel, UreI.
